content: Kaposi's sarcoma remains the most prevalent cancer in Sub-Saharan Africa and is the second most common cancer among HIV-infected individuals globally. The introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has led to a decline in its incidence, but the disease continues to be diagnosed in HIV-positive patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether adding chemotherapy to HAART provides additional benefits compared to HAART alone, and to compare the efficacy of different chemotherapy regimens in HIV-infected adults with severe or progressive Kaposi's sarcoma, both in those receiving HAART and those who are HAART-naive. The review included six randomized controlled trials and three observational studies, involving a total of 792 HIV-infected adults with severe Kaposi's sarcoma. Seven of these studies included patients with varying disease severity, but the analysis focused exclusively on those with severe disease (T1 stage). In studies comparing HAART combined with chemotherapy to HAART alone: One trial involving 100 participants compared HAART plus a combination of doxorubicin, bleomycin, and vincristine (ABV) to HAART alone. It demonstrated a significant reduction in disease progression in the group receiving HAART plus ABV (risk ratio [RR] 0.10; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 0.75). However, there was no statistically significant reduction in mortality or differences in adverse events between the groups. A cohort study involving 129 participants compared HAART plus liposomal anthracyclines to HAART alone. This study showed a non-statistically significant reduction in the incidence of Kaposi's sarcoma immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (RR 0.49; 95% CI 0.16 to 1.55) in the group receiving liposomal anthracyclines. In studies comparing different chemotherapy regimens in patients on HAART: One trial with 49 participants compared paclitaxel to pegylated liposomal doxorubicin. No differences in disease progression were observed between the two groups. Another trial with 46 participants compared pegylated liposomal doxorubicin to liposomal daunorubicin. Neither group showed any cases of progressive Kaposi's sarcoma. In studies conducted during the pre-HAART era, which compared different chemotherapy regimens: A randomized controlled trial involving 227 participants compared liposomal daunorubicin to ABV. There was no significant difference in disease progression (RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.82) or overall response rates between the two regimens. Another trial with 178 participants compared oral etoposide to ABV. No differences in mortality were observed between the two groups. A non-randomized trial compared bleomycin alone to ABV in 24 participants. The ABV group had a higher median survival time and a non-statistically significant reduction in adverse events and disease progression (RR 11; 95% CI 0.67 to 179.29). An additional non-randomized study involving 29 participants compared liposomal doxorubicin to conservative management (which included bleomycin plus vinblastine, vincristine, or single-agent antiretroviral therapy). This study showed a non-statistically significant overall mortality benefit in the liposomal doxorubicin group (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.15). The overall quality of evidence was considered moderate, with limitations due to the small sample sizes of many studies and the low number of events reported. In conclusion, the findings suggest that adding chemotherapy to HAART may reduce disease progression in patients with severe or progressive Kaposi's sarcoma compared to HAART alone. Among patients already on HAART, no significant differences were observed between the efficacy of liposomal doxorubicin, liposomal daunorubicin, and paclitaxel.
